paragraphs.text: Writing appears to have been invented independently at least three, and possibly four, times in human history: in Mesopotamia, in China, in Mesoamerica and perhaps in Egypt. The earliest known system developed in the Sumerian cities of southern Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, around 3200 BC. Surprisingly, it was not created to record stories, laws or religious texts, but to keep accounts.

For several thousand years before writing appeared, people in the region had used small clay tokens of different shapes to represent quantities of goods such as grain, oil and sheep. According to the archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat, these tokens were eventually sealed inside hollow clay balls to guarantee transactions, and their shapes were pressed into the outside of the balls so that the contents could be checked without breaking them. In time, people realised that the marks alone were sufficient, and the tokens became unnecessary.

The early signs were pictures pressed or drawn into wet clay tablets with a reed. Over centuries, they became simplified into groups of wedge-shaped marks, a script now known as cuneiform, from the Latin word for 'wedge'. Crucially, scribes began to use some signs for their sound rather than their meaning, following what is known as the rebus principle. This allowed them to write names and, eventually, complete sentences of spoken language.

Learning cuneiform was difficult, since the system contained several hundred signs, and literacy was restricted to a small class of professional scribes who trained for years in special schools. Many of the surviving tablets are school exercises, complete with the mistakes of students. Yet the script proved remarkably durable: it was used for around 3,000 years to write more than a dozen languages, before being replaced by alphabetic scripts.

Knowledge of how to read cuneiform was lost for nearly two thousand years. It was recovered in the nineteenth century, largely thanks to a long inscription carved on a cliff at Behistun in Iran, which repeats the same text in three languages. Scholars working on the inscription, including the British officer Henry Rawlinson, had deciphered the script by the 1850s, opening up hundreds of thousands of tablets to modern study.
